[Discussion] - How long do you think it will take for humans to start colonizing other planets?

Lowball - 30 years.
Technology is evolving at an astounding rate, and with the possibility of strong AI on the horizon, we could be seeing exponential growth soon.

I think we'll see humans on mars within 30-50 years. I think the impetus will be mining the asteroid belt, but it really depends on a lot of hard to predict economic factors. Like what will we be able to mine cheaply on the moon? Will there be benefits to manufacturing in orbit or on the moon in the next 20 years?

I don't think running out of resources or wild population growth will be a factor this century that pushes us into colonizing the rest of the solar system. Our population growth is slowing and we are getting more efficient at managing our resources. So my bet is economic factors being why we eventually start sending humans to other planets.

I'd guess around 100 years for an ark like ship run entirely by AI with genetic samples it can replicate and 150+ until we have the ability to make a ship that can support a human population while getting us to the nearest habitable system in a reasonable amount of time. You can take 50 years off those estimates if we get our shit together as a species but I wouldn't put money on that happening.

I think the biggest obstacle to space colonization is more about resources than advances in technology. Although technology is definitely helping to ease that burden by working to make space flight cheaper, as long as our only option is sending up rockets it will always consume a lot of fuel. Although the concept of a space elevator has been considered, and would revolutionize humanity's venture into space, there's no viable material at this time to build it with and nothing can be put in the works yet. However, even with rockets we may be able to extract extra-terrestrial resources, process them and manufacture items off-planet. This could create the infrastructure for space colonization while still dealing with the cost of rocket flight.

Mars is on everyone's mind since it's currently the most viable planet for a round-trip mission with current technology. However, the lower gravity, lack of a magnetosphere and harsh radiation will make anyone reconsider actually living there. Further obstructing any colonization is ethical concerns. There may be life on Mars. We may willfully delay sending living creatures to Mars to avoid introducing microbes that could disrupt any attempts to check for existing life. Alternatively, some have proposed a balloon colony over Venus, which would offer gravity equivalent to Earth's as well as air pressure. The only things that would be necessary to sustain the colony would be water and oxygen. Although you probably couldn't send humans down to the surface to obtain any resources, it may be possible for robots to achieve. With humans floating overhead, instructions sent to the robots would only experience short lag times rather than however many hours it might take for instructions to come from Earth.

None of the nearby star systems seem to have any habitable planets either, so candidates for the first colonized planet would probably be in the Solar System. It's probably too soon to properly guess on how long colonization will take, since it's more reliant on how much money people are willing to put into it than how soon technology will be developed.

The closest planet that works like Earth (a water covered atmospheric planet that rests in the goldilocks zone of it's system) is, I think, 13 light years away. It's known as a super earth because it's much bigger than earth (so about as big as the minecraft world, I joke, I kid)

I think with the discovery and the development of our understanding of the Primer Fields and electro-magnetism in space will lead to the development of faster than light space travel, infinite energy sources, and anything else that assist us in our colonization of space.
